title: A Framework for Studying AI Agent Behavior: Evidence from Consumer Choice Experiments
claim: A controlled evaluation pipeline samples realistic choice pairs, then applies targeted interventions to one option to probe decision-making.
layout: 4 panels left-to-right, arrows between stages, numbered callouts on dashed curves
description: A left-to-right workflow titled 'Example of ABxLab Workflow'. The first panel is a mock shopping site, 'OneStopMarket', showing a catalog grid of grey placeholder tiles. An arrow leads to a black-headed 'Sampling Engine' box. It shows three 'vs.' product pairings, two marked with red crosses and one with a green check, captioned '(select realistic choice pairs)'. The next arrow leads to a wireframe page for 'Product A' with stars, a review count, a price, an 'Add to Cart' button and a description. The last panel is a black-headed 'ABxLab Interventions' box with a similar 'Product B' page. Dashed curves in blue, red and teal link numbered markers 1 to 3 to the page elements: a nudge ('best seller'), the price and the rating count. On the right, curved arrows labelled {html} and {edited} frame the three intervention labels: insert nudge, match price to A, match #ratings to A.
caption: Our man-in-the-middle framework (right) consists of an intervention engine which constructs and implements one of several different forms of intervention to one (or none) of the products. Our benchmark (left and middle) consists of (a) a constrained search and selection process for finding plausible product choice pairs (e.g., selecting from the same category, with similar prices and ratings or with perfectly matched ratings), and (b) a binary forced choice paradigm where LLM agents choose which product is better and add it to the cart. See [ref] for real example pairs, and [ref] for details on interventions. The empirical analysis procedure (not pictured) allows us to make robust inferences about the effects of both the natural cues such as price differences and the synthetic ones such as nudges.
abstract: Environments built for people are increasingly operated by a new class of economic actors: LLM-powered software agents making decisions on our behalf. These decisions range from our purchases to travel plans to medical treatment selection. Current evaluations of these agents largely focus on task competence, but we argue for a deeper assessment: how these agents choose when faced with realistic decisions. We introduce ABxLab, a framework for systematically probing agentic choice through controlled manipulations of option attributes and persuasive cues. We apply this to a realistic web-based shopping environment, where we vary prices, ratings, and psychological nudges, all of which are factors long known to shape human choice. We find that agent decisions shift predictably and substantially in response, revealing that agents are strongly biased choosers even without being subject to the cognitive constraints that shape human biases. This susceptibility reveals both risk and opportunity: risk, because agentic consumers may inherit and amplify human biases; opportunity, because consumer choice provides a powerful testbed for a behavioral science of AI agents, just as it has for the study of human behavior. We release our framework as an open benchmark for rigorous, scalable evaluation of agent decision-making.
